domain_reasoning: Besides talking, the time goes into looking up product, price or policy information in knowledge bases and account screens.
length_reasoning: A simple factual question is answered in a couple of minutes; a multi-part product comparison or lookup across systems takes ten or more.
review_reasoning: A QA reviewer listens to the recording, mostly sped up, and checks the answer against the knowledge base; longer calls take proportionally longer.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong answer about a product or service leads to a callback or complaint and can be corrected.
context_reasoning: Needs the employer's product details and policies, learned over a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: Most time goes into reading and consolidating tester feedback and writing the report, with filing defects a smaller share.
length_reasoning: A small round with a few testers takes an hour or two; a large round with many reports to dedupe and file takes most of a day.
review_reasoning: The QA manager reads the report and spot-checks raw feedback and filed defects against it; a large round needs many items checked.
stakes_reasoning: Missed or misreported findings can let defects through to release, but are usually caught later and fixed.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the product, its known issues and the team's defect conventions, built over a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The core work is reading policy terms and the loss report, then recording the decision in the claims system; reading dominates.
length_reasoning: A clear-cut loss is decided in about fifteen minutes; a loss with exclusions, endorsements or ambiguous facts takes a couple of hours.
review_reasoning: The adjuster reads the loss facts and the relevant clauses and checks the reasoning; complex cases need exclusions and endorsements checked closely.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong coverage decision means a wrongly paid or denied claim, with financial and regulatory exposure.
context_reasoning: Needs the insurer's policy forms, claims rules and procedures, learned over months.

domain_reasoning: Writing test cases and scenarios from requirements is mostly document writing, with the repository entry a minor step.
length_reasoning: A small area takes a day; a regression or database-impact suite for a large release takes several days.
review_reasoning: The QA lead reads the cases against requirements and checks coverage and gaps; a large suite takes much longer.
stakes_reasoning: Gaps in a suite let bugs escape, but the cost shows up later and is usually found in later testing or production at modest cost.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the product's behaviour, requirements and the team's test conventions, built over weeks to months.

domain_reasoning: The worker runs commands, checks consoles and status pages and files tickets, all operating systems and tools.
length_reasoning: A clean round across a few systems takes about fifteen minutes; one with several errors to investigate and log takes over an hour.
review_reasoning: The supervisor reads the recorded results and opens any tickets; verifying the checks themselves needs spot-checks of systems.
stakes_reasoning: A missed error is usually found when users report it, and is fixed with limited disruption.
context_reasoning: Needs the organisation's systems inventory and what normal looks like, learned in a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: Apart from talking, the time goes into reproducing the issue, reading logs and operating the product and tools.
length_reasoning: A familiar problem is diagnosed in ten minutes; a hard one needing reproduction and logs takes over an hour.
review_reasoning: A reviewer must follow the session recording at near real time to judge the diagnosis, and check the agreed next steps.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong diagnosis sends the customer or developers down the wrong path and costs rework, but is reversible.
context_reasoning: Needs the product's internals and customer deployments, built over months.

domain_reasoning: Apart from talking, the time goes into operating the user's machine, admin consoles and ticketing tools.
length_reasoning: Simple password or how-to questions take a few minutes; a real fault takes up to half an hour.
review_reasoning: A supervisor listens to the call or reads the chat, sped up, and checks the ticket; longer contacts take longer.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong fix leaves the user unable to work briefly and prompts a repeat contact, easily reversed.
context_reasoning: Needs the organisation's standard software, setup and policies, learned in a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The work is typing into the CRM or account system and selecting codes and fields while the customer talks.
length_reasoning: Notes are entered alongside the contact, so the item spans the whole contact from a short query to a long complaint.
review_reasoning: A QA reviewer reads the notes against the call recording, partly sped up; short contacts are quick.
stakes_reasoning: Poor notes cause confusion for later agents and repeat contacts, usually fixed cheaply.
context_reasoning: Needs the company's note formats, contact codes and systems, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: Writing steps, severity and attaching evidence in a tracker is mostly composing text, though it happens inside the tracker.
length_reasoning: An obvious bug takes ten minutes to write up; a hard-to-reproduce one with logs and narrowing takes an hour.
review_reasoning: A developer or triage lead reads the ticket and follows the steps, sometimes reproducing; a complex report takes longer.
stakes_reasoning: A weak report costs developer time and delay but is cheap to correct.
context_reasoning: Needs the product's behaviour and the team's tracker conventions, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: Most time goes into entering the request into the billing or account system and sending a confirmation.
length_reasoning: A simple address change takes five minutes; a contract or discontinuance needing verification and several screens takes half an hour.
review_reasoning: A reviewer compares the entered record to the request on screen; complex orders need more fields checked.
stakes_reasoning: An error causes a wrong bill or service action, noticed by the customer and correctable, though a wrong discontinuance can be costly.
context_reasoning: Needs the company's order forms, systems and rules, learned in weeks.

domain_reasoning: The worker runs tests and operates the machine and applications to confirm it works.
length_reasoning: A simple install check takes five minutes; a repair or major change needing thorough testing takes close to an hour.
review_reasoning: The lead reads the ticket note and sometimes spot-checks the machine; longer verifications need more checks.
stakes_reasoning: A missed fault means the user returns with the same problem, a small cost.
context_reasoning: Needs the organisation's standard builds and applications, learned in a few weeks.

domain_reasoning: The output is a written note after evaluating the build, mostly writing and reading.
length_reasoning: Writing up a small feature takes half an hour; a large build with many observations takes several hours.
review_reasoning: Developers read the note and verify points against the build; a longer note needs more checking.
stakes_reasoning: Poor feedback causes wasted developer effort or missed usability issues, fixable later.
context_reasoning: Needs the product's intended behaviour and users, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: The work is matching records and preparing the invoice in the billing system.
length_reasoning: A simple full return takes ten minutes; a partial return with price or quantity discrepancies takes up to an hour.
review_reasoning: Accounts receivable compares the invoice to the requisition and original invoice line by line; longer ones need more lines checked.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong return invoice means a wrong credit or charge, a financial error corrected through adjustment but sometimes sizeable.
context_reasoning: Needs the company's pricing, return rules and billing systems, learned over weeks.

domain_reasoning: Pulling data from the tracker, building counts and charts and writing commentary is mostly operating the tracker and spreadsheets.
length_reasoning: A routine weekly report takes under an hour; an end-of-sprint report with analysis of trends and blockers takes several hours.
review_reasoning: The manager checks counts against the tracker and reads the blocker discussion; a detailed report takes longer.
stakes_reasoning: Wrong counts can mislead release decisions, but are visible and corrected quickly.
context_reasoning: Needs the project's tracker setup, severity definitions and team context, learned over weeks.

unit_flag_reason: Orders and account cancellations differ in kind and length (cancellations often involve retention talk), so the item mixes two types of work.
domain_reasoning: Besides talking, the time goes into entering the order or cancellation in the order or billing system.
length_reasoning: A simple order or cancellation takes about five minutes; one with several products, payment details or retention attempts takes twenty.
review_reasoning: A reviewer listens to the contact and checks the entered order or cancellation record against it.
stakes_reasoning: A wrong order or cancellation causes a wrong shipment or billing and a complaint, though a wrongful cancellation or charge can be costly.
context_reasoning: Needs the company's products, order system and cancellation policies, learned in weeks.

domain_reasoning: Preparing a strategy and schedule is mostly reading scope documents and writing a plan.
length_reasoning: A small release plan takes half a day; a large project strategy with stakeholder negotiation takes several days of active work.
review_reasoning: The QA or project manager reads the plan and checks it against scope and dates; a big plan needs detailed checking of estimates.
stakes_reasoning: A flawed plan causes missed dates or weak test coverage, costly but visible early and adjustable.
context_reasoning: Needs knowledge of the project, team capacity and release process, built over months.
